{{Nihongo|{{ill|Iki Gokoku Shrine|ja|壱岐神社|en:draft|Iki Gokoku Shrine}}|壱岐護国神社|Iki Gokoku Jinja}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Iki Province|en|Iki Province|qid=Q1052938|lt=Iki Province}} {{ill|Japan|en|Japan}}.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Iki City Tourism Federation Website|url=http://shrine.ikikankou.com/english/jinja/|access-date=2024-03-28|website=Iki City Tourism Federation Website|language=en|text=Iki Shrine/Ikigokoku Shrine Shonioketokiko & 2 other gods 駐車場ありトイレあり四十二社巡り 264 Seto-ura, Ashibe-cho, Iki-shi 〒811-5461MAP Regarding Goshuin Reservations There are goshuin that have been written and placed at the shrine in advance. After visiting the shrine, please offer 300 yen and take one. ☎0920-45-1276 ※Depending on the availability of the priest, there are times when you may not be able to receive a goshuin. Thank you for your kind understanding.}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=【壱岐神社】アクセス・営業時間・料金情報 - じゃらんnet|url=https://www.jalan.net/kankou/spt_42423ag2130011542/|access-date=2024-03-28|website=www.jalan.net|language=ja}}</ref> It is also called Iki Shrine.<ref name=":1" /> It is a {{ill|Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrines|en|lt=Gokoku shrine}}, or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine}}. They were renamed from {{ill|Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrines|en|lt=Shokonsha}} in 1939.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}}</ref> However it also worships other deities than war dead, hence sometimes being called just Iki Shrine.<ref name=":1" />

Although some of the deities of each shrine overlap with those of {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine|en}},{{Efn|Yasukuni Shrine also enshrines the war dead as Heroic Spirits and was renamed from Tokyo Shokonsha, but includes {{ill|Empire of Japan|Empire of the Empire of Japan|en}}, [[:en:Citizens|Citizens]], {{ill|Koreans|en|Koreans|lt=Koreans}}, {{ill|Taiwanese people|en|Taiwanese people|qid=Q707133|lt=Taiwanese}}, etc. The difference is that people from anywhere are eligible to be enshrined.}} the deities of each shrine are not separated from Yasukuni Shrine, and they perform their own rituals by inviting the souls of their own deities. However there are some exceptions, such as {{ill|Hida Gokoku Shrine|en|Hida Gokoku Shrine}} in Gifu Prefecture and {{ill|Iki Gokoku Shrine|ja|壱岐神社|en:draft|Iki Gokoku Shrine}} in Nagasaki Prefecture. 

It was rennovated in 2005.<ref name="www.ikiweb.com">{{Cite web|title=壱岐神社|url=http://www.ikiweb.com/ikijinjya/|access-date=2024-03-28|website=www.ikiweb.com}}</ref>
== History ==

{{ill|Shōni Suketoki|ja|少弐資時|qid=Q11464745}} was a war hero against the mongols<ref name="www.ikiweb.com" />. He died in 1281.<ref name=":0" />

The stone mound called "Shounii-sama" (ショウニイさま) was recognized in 1898 (the 31st year of the Meiji era) as the grave of {{ill|Shōni Suketoki|ja|少弐資時|qid=Q11464745}}, embodying the faith of local people who have passed down and protected it for over 600 years.<ref name=":0" />

1944: Construction of the main hall  

1948: Enshrinement festival for the deities  

1952: Iki Gokoku Shrine Festival  

1955: A man was enshrined who died in the war from illness.<ref name="www.ikiweb.com" />  

1956: On November 8, a portion of the spirits of those from Iki County who died in war or from illness were enshrined at Yasukuni Shrine. Approval was granted to also call it Iki Gokoku Shrine.  

== Main Festivals ==
January 1: New Year's Festival  

February 11: National Foundation Day Festival  

April 12: Eve of the Grand Festival  

April 13: Grand Festival  

Third Sunday of April: Regular Grand Festival, Offering Ceremony, Tomb Festival  

May 27: Navy Memorial Service  

August 15: End of War Memorial Festival  

December 31: New Year's Eve Festival
